Example script analyzing the MIT Social Evolution data with `R`'s `goldfish`
package.
Models inspired by section 7 of:

> Stadtfeld & Block (2017), "Interactions, Actors and Time: Dynamic Network
> Actor Models for Relational Events", Sociological Science, 2017, 4(1):
> 318-352. DOI: 10.15195/v4.a14

# Step 0: Load package and data

First, we load the `goldfish` package.
`goldfish` consumes a **single data object**: a `stocnet` (from the
[`manynet`](https://stocnet.github.io/manynet/) package) that bundles the node
set, the network layers, and any attribute changes together.
The package ships the Social Evolution study prebuilt in that shape as
`social_evolution`, ready to model.
You can find out more about this dataset, its format, and its origins by calling
its documentation.


``` r
library(goldfish)
data("social_evolution")
# ?social_evolution
social_evolution
#> # A tibble: 84 × 4
#>   label    active floor gradeType
#>   <chr>    <lgl>  <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 Actor 47 TRUE       4         3
#> 2 Actor 57 TRUE       2         1
#> 3 Actor 9  TRUE       9         2
#> 4 Actor 68 TRUE       8         1
#> 5 Actor 23 TRUE       5         2
#> 6 Actor 49 TRUE       7         4
#> # ℹ 78 more rows
#> # A tibble: 1,205 × 5
#>    from    to time                weight layer     
#>   <int> <int> <dttm>               <dbl> <chr>     
#> 1     1    64 2008-09-09 00:00:00      1 friendship
#> 2     2    64 2008-09-09 00:00:00      1 friendship
#> 3     3    67 2008-09-09 00:00:00      1 friendship
#> 4     4    62 2008-09-09 00:00:00      1 friendship
#> 5     5    62 2008-09-09 00:00:00      1 friendship
#> 6     6    62 2008-09-09 00:00:00      1 friendship
#> # ℹ 1,199 more rows
```

The object carries two **layers** over one node set of 84 actors: `calls`, the
time-stamped phone calls (an `"event"` layer), and `friendship`, the survey
nominations (a `"panel"` layer). We model the `calls` layer here: a model names
its dependent process on the formula's left-hand side, and `social_evolution`
also records `calls` as the optional default **focal** layer.

# Preamble: Run a quick DyNAM in three lines

We use an `R` version higher than 4.2.0 to compile the vignettes.
The native pipe operator is available in `R` from version 4.1.0.

With the prebuilt object there is nothing to assemble -- the focal `calls` layer
names the dependent process on the left-hand side of the formula:


``` r
mod00Rate <- estimate_dynam(
  calls ~ indeg + outdeg,
  sub_model = "rate",
  data = social_evolution
)
#> ℹ `sub_model = "rate"` models the waiting times between events; a time
#>   intercept has been added.
#> ℹ Use `sub_model = "rate_ordered"` to model only the order of the events
#>   (ordinal likelihood).
summary(mod00Rate)
#>

#> estimate_dynam(x = calls ~ indeg + outdeg, sub_model = "rate", 
#>     data = social_evolution)

#> outdeg/calls   0.256839   0.029094    8.8279 < 2.2e-16 ***
```

# Step 1: How the data object is built

The prebuilt `social_evolution` object was assembled from the raw data frames
that ship as `Social_Evolution`. Understanding that construction workflow lets
you bring your own data into `goldfish`. Everything here uses `manynet`, the
package that owns the `stocnet` data structure.


``` r
library(manynet)
data("Social_Evolution")
head(actors)
#>     label present floor gradeType
#> 1 Actor 1    TRUE     3         5
#> 2 Actor 2    TRUE     5         1
#> 3 Actor 3    TRUE     5         2
#> 4 Actor 4    TRUE     2         2
#> 5 Actor 5    TRUE     4         1
#> 6 Actor 6    TRUE     4         2
head(calls)
#>                  time   sender receiver increment
#> 1 2008-09-06 20:37:50 Actor 72 Actor 50         1
#> 2 2008-09-11 03:16:14 Actor 43 Actor 51         1
#> 3 2008-09-19 00:31:33 Actor 43 Actor 51         1
#> 4 2008-09-19 00:58:02 Actor 43 Actor 22         1
#> 5 2008-09-19 01:21:04 Actor 43 Actor 55         1
#> 6 2008-09-19 18:20:43 Actor 43 Actor 51         1
head(friendship)
#>         time   sender receiver replace
#> 1 2008-09-09 Actor 47  Actor 2       1
#> 3 2008-09-09 Actor 57  Actor 2       1
#> 4 2008-09-09  Actor 9 Actor 38       1
#> 5 2008-09-09 Actor 68 Actor 40       1
#> 6 2008-09-09 Actor 23 Actor 40       1
#> 7 2008-09-09 Actor 49 Actor 40       1
```

`actors` holds the node attributes: `label` (the identifier), `present`
(renamed `active` in the stocnet), the `floor` of residence, and `gradeType`
(1 = freshmen to 5 = graduate). `calls` and `friendship` are event lists with
`time`, `sender`, and `receiver`; `calls` carries an `increment` column (the
tie strength accumulates) while `friendship` carries a `replace` column (each
survey wave overwrites the value).

## Step 1a: One layer at a time

`as_stocnet()` turns an event list (or an adjacency matrix) into a single-layer
`stocnet`. `from_ties()` merges several layers over one shared node set, and
`join_nodes()` attaches the actor attributes.


``` r
social_evolution_built <- from_ties(
  as_stocnet(friendship),
  as_stocnet(calls),
  layer_names = c("friendship", "calls")
) |>
  join_nodes(actors) |>
  rename_nodes()
#> Joining with `by = join_by(label)`
social_evolution_built
#> 
#> ── # friendship + calls ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> # A dynamic, labelled, multiplex, undirected network of 84 nodes and 766
#> friendship ties and 439 call ties (378 parallel) from 2008-09-06 20:37:50 to
#> 2008-10-19
#> 
#> ── Nodes
#> # A tibble: 84 × 4
#>   label    active floor gradeType
#>   <chr>    <lgl>  <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 Actor 47 TRUE       4         3
#> 2 Actor 57 TRUE       2         1
#> 3 Actor 9  TRUE       9         2
#> 4 Actor 68 TRUE       8         1
#> 5 Actor 23 TRUE       5         2
#> 6 Actor 49 TRUE       7         4
#> # ℹ 78 more rows
#> 
#> ── Ties
#> # A tibble: 1,205 × 5
#>    from    to time                weight layer     
#>   <int> <int> <dttm>               <dbl> <chr>     
#> 1     1    64 2008-09-09 00:00:00      1 friendship
#> 2     2    64 2008-09-09 00:00:00      1 friendship
#> 3     3    67 2008-09-09 00:00:00      1 friendship
#> 4     4    62 2008-09-09 00:00:00      1 friendship

#> 6     6    62 2008-09-09 00:00:00      1 friendship
#> # ℹ 1,199 more rows
#> 
```

## Step 1b: Declaring the layer semantics

`add_info()` records the metadata `goldfish` needs: whether each layer is
`directed`, each layer's `observation` type, and -- optionally -- a default
`focal` layer. `focal` is not required: the formula's left-hand side (or a
specification's `layer`) names the dependent, and that modeled layer drives the
rest. `goldfish` models two observation types:

- an `"event"` layer is a stream of time-stamped relational events (the
  `calls`), and
- a `"panel"` layer is a covariate observed at survey waves (the
  `friendship`), whose rows are applied at their wave times.


``` r
social_evolution_built <- add_info(
  social_evolution_built,
  name = "Social Evolution MIT",
  # focal is optional -- the formula LHS names the dependent. Recorded here only
  # to set the shipped object's default; drop it and `calls ~ ...` still works.
  focal = "calls",
  directed = c(friendship = TRUE, calls = TRUE),
  observation = c(friendship = "panel", calls = "event")
)
```

This reproduces the shipped `social_evolution`, so the rest of the vignette
simply uses the prebuilt object.

A few conventions worth knowing when you assemble your own data:

- **History with `time = NA`.** Ties that hold *before* the observation window
  (for example, an initial adjacency matrix) enter with `time = NA`; they seed
  the starting state instead of becoming events. (Social Evolution starts from
  an empty network, so it has no history rows -- the Fisheries vignette shows
  this.)
- **Panel dissolutions are explicit.** A `"panel"` layer only knows what its
  rows say: to *remove* a tie at a wave you must include an explicit value-`0`
  row. `goldfish` cannot infer a dissolution from the absence of a row.
- **Mode sets restrict a layer.** With a single node set every layer spans all
  the nodes. In a multimodal node set an *undeclared* layer still spans **all**
  modes; declare `sender`/`receiver` mode sets in `add_info()` to make a layer
  one-mode over a subset, or two-mode across disjoint sets.
- **Tie-break with `order`.** If two events with the same `replace` target hit
  the exact same timestamp, add an integer `order` column so their sequence is
  unambiguous (again, see the Fisheries vignette).

## Missing data

goldfish imputes a missing value during preprocessing, before any effect is
evaluated, by a single rule that depends on the object's *shape* and on *when*
the value is missing:

| shape | at the start of the window | during the walk |
|---|---|---|
| dyad (network) | `NA` is no tie (zero) | a missing `increment`/`replace` is no tie (zero) |
| global | aborts | aborts |
| node, numeric | mean of the node's mode category, itself excluded | the same rule, on the state at the event's time |
| node, categorical | most common value in the node's mode category, itself excluded | the same rule, on the state at the event's time |

A missing tie is the *absence* of a tie -- a definition, not a summary. A
global attribute has a single value and so no pool to summarize from: a missing
global value aborts at schedule construction rather than being replaced by an
arbitrary zero.

An imputed value joins the process state exactly as an observed one does, so a
nodal value missing *after* the start of the window is summarized from a pool
that may already contain earlier *imputed* values. Single imputation treats
those as observed and understates the uncertainty the missingness carries; when
that uncertainty matters to the conclusions, impute *before* building the
goldfish object and combine several fits under Rubin's rules (see the
`goldfish_data` help page's *Missing data* section).

## Intermediate step: Visualization

While not a required part of the modeling process,
we highly recommend the visualization of your data for analytic and
diagnostic purposes.
`goldfish` exports `network_state_at()` and `nodes_state_at()` to evaluate a
layer's network -- and the node attributes -- at any time point, honoring the
history and each layer's update semantics.

We can use these to visually compare the call network at two (or more)
different time periods using `migraph`. See the `migraph` package documentation
for additional information about network visualization.


``` r
library(igraph)
library(ggraph)
library(migraph)
# The network at half time
half_time <- calls$time[floor(nrow(calls) / 2)]
callNetworkHlf <- network_state_at(social_evolution, "calls", time = half_time)
floorHlf <- nodes_state_at(social_evolution, time = half_time)$floor

callNetworkHlf <- callNetworkHlf |>
  as_igraph() |>
  add_node_attribute("floor", floorHlf)

graphr(callNetworkHlf, labels = FALSE, layout = "fr") +
  geom_node_point(aes(color = as.factor(floor)), size = 2, show.legend = FALSE)
```

![plot of chunk plot-teaching1](teaching/plot-teaching1-1.png)

``` r

# The tie strength at the end
end_time <- max(calls$time) + 1
callNetworkEnd <- network_state_at(social_evolution, "calls", time = end_time)
table(callNetworkEnd)
#> callNetworkEnd
#>    0    1    2    3    4    6    7    8    9   10   11   13   15   64  115 
#> 6972   36   13   10    8    1    5    3    1    1    1    2    1    1    1
```

# Step 2: Specify and estimate model

The second step is to specify and fit a model to this data.
This step can be broken up into several stages:

-   **Step 2a**. *Formula*: Specify a model formula from the effects and
  variables available

-   **Step 2b**. *Preprocessing*: Calculate the change statistics associated
  with these effects

-   **Step 2c**. *Estimation*: Fit an appropriate model to these statistics

However, in goldfish we also have the option of accelerating this process and
using memory more efficiently by combining these three sub-steps in one.
Nonetheless, it can be helpful to think of 2a separately, and
recognize steps 2b and 2c as goldfish does them.

## Step 2a. Formula

We specify our model using the standard R formula format like:

`layer ~ effects(process_state_element)`

The left-hand side names the **focal layer** (`calls`); an effect's argument
names another **layer** (`friendship`) or a **node attribute** (`floor`,
`gradeType`) by its bare name. An effect with no argument reads the focal layer.

We can see which effects are currently available and how to specify them here:


``` r
vignette("goldfishEffects")
```

Let's start with the simplest model we can imagine:


``` r
simpleFormulaChoice <- calls ~ tie(friendship)
```

What are we testing here?
Do individuals call their friends more than non-friends?

## Step 2b and 2c. Preprocessing and Estimation

Now to estimate this model, we use the `?estimate` function.
For now, only need to worry about the `formula` and the `model`,
`subModel` type (DyNAM-choice).


``` r
mod01Choice <- estimate_dynam(
  simpleFormulaChoice,
  sub_model = "choice",
  data = social_evolution
)
summary(mod01Choice)
#> 
#> Call:
#> estimate_dynam(x = calls ~ tie(friendship), sub_model = "choice", 
#>     data = social_evolution)
#> 
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#>                Estimate Std. Error z-value  Pr(>|z|)    
#> tie/friendship  4.02538    0.12513   32.17 < 2.2e-16 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> 
#>   Return code 1: gradient close to zero
#>     score (rel. norm): 9.83e-11    step (max|update|): 1.98e-09
#>   1 parameter estimated  
#>   Log-Likelihood: -1288.7
#>   AIC:  2579.4 
#>   AICc: 2579.4 
#>   BIC:  2583.5 
#>   model: "DyNAM" sub_model: "choice"
```

Ok, as fascinating as that was, perhaps we can test how robust
this finding is in the presence of plausible controls.


``` r
complexFormulaChoice <-
  calls ~ inertia(calls) + recip(calls) +
    tie(friendship) + recip(friendship) +
    same(gradeType) + same(floor)

mod02Choice <- estimate_dynam(
  complexFormulaChoice,
  sub_model = "choice",
  data = social_evolution
)
#> Warning: ℹ Missing data has been detected. The mean is used to impute numeric
#>   attributes.
summary(mod02Choice)
#> 
#> Call:
#> estimate_dynam(x = calls ~ inertia(calls) + recip(calls) + tie(friendship) +
```

### Rate model

How do individual properties affect the rate of action of individuals?
(Step 1 of the model)

Let us again define a simple formula that only depends on individuals' degree
in the friendship network


``` r
simpleFormulaRate <- calls ~ indeg(friendship)
mod01Rate <- estimate_dynam(
  simpleFormulaRate,
  sub_model = "rate",
  data = social_evolution
)
#> ℹ `sub_model = "rate"` models the waiting times between events; a time
#>   intercept has been added.
#> ℹ Use `sub_model = "rate_ordered"` to model only the order of the events
#>   (ordinal likelihood).
```

#### Remark:

Sometimes, the default values for the algorithm are not enough
to reach convergence.
The default values for the estimation algorithm are set by the function
`set_algorithm_newton()`, you can take a look to the different arguments and
options that can be modified for the estimation algorithm taking a look to its
documentation.
We can remedy this by increasing the number of iterations setting a different
value using the `control_algo` argument:


``` r
mod01Rate <- estimate_dynam(
  simpleFormulaRate,
  sub_model = "rate",
  data = social_evolution,
  control_algo = set_algorithm_newton(max_iterations = 40)
)
#> ℹ `sub_model = "rate"` models the waiting times between events; a time
#>   intercept has been added.
#> ℹ Use `sub_model = "rate_ordered"` to model only the order of the events
#>   (ordinal likelihood).
summary(mod01Rate)
#> 
#> Call:
#> estimate_dynam(x = calls ~ indeg(friendship), sub_model = "rate", 
#>     data = social_evolution, control_algo = set_algorithm_newton(max_iterations = 40))
#> 
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#>                    Estimate Std. Error  z-value  Pr(>|z|)    
#> Intercept        -14.358176   0.095684 -150.059 < 2.2e-16 ***
#> indeg/friendship   0.166207   0.012438   13.363 < 2.2e-16 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> 
#>   Return code 1: gradient close to zero
#>     score (rel. norm): 8.14e-12    step (max|update|): 1.34e-10
#>   2 parameters estimated  
#>   Log-Likelihood: -6255.8
#>   AIC:  12516 
#>   AICc: 12516 
#>   BIC:  12524 
#>   model: "DyNAM" sub_model: "rate"
```

What if we include additional structural effects?
Let us add the in and out degree of the nodes in the call network

``` r
complexFormulaRate <-
  calls ~ indeg(calls) + outdeg(calls) + indeg(friendship)

mod02Rate <- estimate_dynam(
  complexFormulaRate,
  sub_model = "rate",
  data = social_evolution
)
#> ℹ `sub_model = "rate"` models the waiting times between events; a time
#>   intercept has been added.
#> ℹ Use `sub_model = "rate_ordered"` to model only the order of the events
#>   (ordinal likelihood).
summary(mod02Rate)
```

#### Right-censored intervals

Recall that it is important to add a time intercept when estimating models with
right-censored intervals (as discussed in Stadtfeld & Block, 2017).
Adding an intercept is as easy as including a 1 to the formula:


``` r
interceptFormulaRate <-
  calls ~ 1 + indeg(calls) + outdeg(calls) + indeg(friendship)

mod03Rate <- estimate_dynam(
  interceptFormulaRate,
  sub_model = "rate",
  data = social_evolution
)
summary(mod03Rate)
#> 
#> Call:
#> estimate_dynam(x = calls ~ 1 + indeg(calls) + outdeg(calls) + 
#>     indeg(friendship), sub_model = "rate", data = social_evolution)
#> 
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#>                    Estimate Std. Error   z-value  Pr(>|z|)    
#> Intercept        -14.380373   0.095669 -150.3135 < 2.2e-16 ***
#> indeg/calls        0.695555   0.063115   11.0204 < 2.2e-16 ***
#> outdeg/calls       0.234633   0.030153    7.7814 7.105e-15 ***
#> indeg/friendship   0.054792   0.015049    3.6409 0.0002716 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> 
#>   Return code 1: gradient close to zero
#>     score (rel. norm): 3.84e-11    step (max|update|): 6.24e-10
#>   4 parameters estimated  
#>   Log-Likelihood: -6003.1
#>   AIC:  12014 
#>   AICc: 12014 
#>   BIC:  12031 
#>   model: "DyNAM" sub_model: "rate"
```

Note that $1 / \exp({\beta_{intercept}})$ is the waiting time
without any covariates, or how long it takes to make the next phone call
if everything else is set to 0.
Therefore, the larger the intercept the shorter the waiting time.
For example, an intercept of -14 means a waiting time of
$1 / e^{-14} = 334$ hours.
The baseline waiting time between two events in hours:

Effects get compact, disambiguated names in the coefficient vector -- here
`odeg` is the call out-degree and `ideg_cal` the call in-degree (the friendship
in-degree becomes `ideg_fri`):


``` r
mod03RateCoef <- coef(mod03Rate)
mod03RateCoef
#>    Intercept     ideg_cal         odeg     ideg_fri 
#> -14.38037286   0.69555509   0.23463293   0.05479232

1 / exp(mod03RateCoef[["Intercept"]]) / 3600
#> [1] 488.6682
# or days:
1 / exp(mod03RateCoef[["Intercept"]]) / 86400
#> [1] 20.36118

# But what if it is not just a random call?
# Expected waiting time of those who have five outgoing call ties
# (five different actors)
1 / exp(
  mod03RateCoef[["Intercept"]] + mod03RateCoef[["odeg"]] * 5
) / 3600
#> [1] 151.1872
# Expected waiting time of those who have five outgoing and incoming call ties
# (five different actors)
1 / exp(
  mod03RateCoef[["Intercept"]] +
    mod03RateCoef[["odeg"]] * 5 +
    mod03RateCoef[["ideg_cal"]] * 5
) / 3600
#> [1] 4.66806
```

### Windows effects

Remember our `calls` process state accumulates actions in time,
but some older actions may no longer be relevant to current action.
Let's see whether it is really just recent partners that matter
by adding extra effects with a window of... how long?
Let us try 5 minutes $= 5 * 60 = 300s$


``` r
windowFormulaRate <-
  calls ~ 1 + indeg(calls) + outdeg(calls) +
    indeg(calls, window = 300) +
    outdeg(calls, window = 300) +
    indeg(friendship)

mod04Rate <- estimate_dynam(
  windowFormulaRate,
  sub_model = "rate",
  data = social_evolution
)
summary(mod04Rate)
#> 
#> Call:
#> estimate_dynam(x = calls ~ 1 + indeg(calls) + outdeg(calls) +

#> outdeg/calls [wdw]  -0.767499   0.116642   -6.5800 4.706e-11 ***
#> indeg/friendship     0.083772   0.015289    5.4794 4.268e-08 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
```

Of course, you can also add windows to the choice formula!


``` r
windowFormulaChoice <-
  calls ~ inertia(calls) + recip(calls) +
    inertia(calls, window = 300) +
    recip(calls, window = 300) +
    tie(friendship) + recip(friendship) +
    same(gradeType) + same(floor)

mod03Choice <- estimate_dynam(
  windowFormulaChoice,
  sub_model = "choice",
  data = social_evolution
)
#> Warning: ℹ Missing data has been detected. The mean is used to impute numeric
#>   attributes.
summary(mod03Choice)
#> 
#> Call:
#> estimate_dynam(x = calls ~ inertia(calls) + recip(calls) + inertia(calls, 
#>     window = 300) + recip(calls, window = 300) + tie(friendship) +

#> tie/friendship       1.50593    0.27206  5.5354 3.105e-08 ***

```

All this shows you that you can specify different formula
for the rate and choice components of the model.
This is a key advantage of the DyNAM!

When comparing the information criteria (AIC / BIC) of the different models,
we see that the time windows explain a lot


``` r
# Compare different specifications of the subModel = "choice"
AIC(mod02Choice, mod03Choice)
#>             df      AIC
#> mod02Choice  6 1287.912
#> mod03Choice  8 1147.804

# Compare different specifications of the subModel = "rate"
AIC(mod03Rate, mod04Rate)
#>           df      AIC
#> mod03Rate  4 12014.20
#> mod04Rate  6 10963.75
```

### REM with `goldfish`

`goldfish` does not only run DyNAMs; it also runs REMs (Butts, 2008).
We can now also run REMs using the right-censored intervals as introduced in
Stadtfeld & Block (2017).
An equivalent model specification to the DyNAM model we estimated above,
including the rate and choice sub-models, is:



``` r
allFormulaREM <-
  calls ~
    1 + indeg(calls, type = "ego") + outdeg(calls, type = "ego") +
    indeg(friendship, type = "ego") +
    inertia(calls) + recip(calls) +
    inertia(calls, window = 300) + recip(calls, window = 300) +
    tie(friendship) + recip(friendship) +
    same(gradeType) + same(floor)
```

And we can estimate this model, to speed up estimation, we can use any of the
two `C` implementations of the estimation algorithm.
Setting the option `backend` on the `control_algo` argument, we can choose
which version of the `C` code to use.
`"cpp"` implements the same algorithm as
the `"r"` one implemented in plain `R` code that reduces the memory use
by exploiting the sparsity of the dyads that change the effects' statistics
after each event.
`"gather"` implements a version with an overhead of memory use,
representing the data in a more usual tabular way but reducing time estimation.


``` r
mod01REM <- estimate_rem(
  allFormulaREM,
  data = social_evolution,
  control_algo =
    set_algorithm_newton(initial_damping = 40, backend = "cpp")
)
```


``` r
mod01REM <- estimate_rem(
  allFormulaREM,
  data = social_evolution,
  control_algo = set_algorithm_newton(backend = "gather")
)
#> Warning: ℹ Missing data has been detected. The mean is used to impute numeric
#>   attributes.

summary(mod01REM)
#>
```

# Step 4: Diagnose the model

Estimation says what the coefficients are. The next question is whether the
model that produced them is one to believe. This is a short tour; the
[diagnostics vignette](diagnostics.html) is the full treatment.



## Which events surprised the model

Deviance residuals are large where the model did badly. Ranked, they name the
events worth looking at.


``` r
mod01ChoiceDiag <- estimate_dynam(
  complexFormulaChoice,
  sub_model = "choice",
  data = social_evolution,
  return_preprocessed = TRUE
)
#> Warning: ℹ Missing data has been detected. The mean is used to impute numeric
#>   attributes.
#> ℹ The fit carries the preprocessed statistics it was estimated from (about
#>   399.8 Kb).

dev <- residuals(mod01ChoiceDiag, type = "deviance")
worst <- order(abs(dev), decreasing = TRUE)[1:3]
data.frame(
  event = worst,
  deviance = round(dev[worst], 2),
  fitted = round(fitted(mod01ChoiceDiag, type = "outcome")[worst], 4)
)
#>   event deviance fitted
#> 1   168    16.98  2e-04
#> 2    87    16.92  2e-04
#> 3   255    15.95  3e-04
```

A small fitted probability on a realized event is exactly what a large
deviance residual reports: the model thought that call unlikely and it
happened.

## Is each effect's contribution spread over the sequence?

At the maximum the per-event scores sum to zero, so each effect's cumulative
score process starts and ends at zero. Under a well-specified model it is a
Brownian bridge; a path that wanders is an effect whose contribution is
concentrated somewhere in the sequence.


``` r
# Qualified deliberately. This vignette attaches migraph further up, and
# migraph exports a (deprecated) `test_gof` of its own, so the bare name
# resolves to whichever package was attached last. RSiena publishes the same
# three test names too. `::` is the reliable route whenever more than one
# stocnet package is loaded.
goldfish::test_gof(mod01ChoiceDiag)
#> ── <goldfishGOF> ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Model "DyNAM" · sub-model "choice" · backend "cpp"
#> 439 intervals, 439 dependent events; 6 effects tested.
#> Supremum of the standardized cumulative score process, against the Kolmogorov
#> distribution on the event clock.
#> # A tibble: 6 × 7
#>   index term             coefficient statistic p_value scale  rank
#>   <int> <chr>            <chr>           <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl> <int>
#> 1     1 inertia/calls    inrt            0.929 0.354    6.78     5
#> 2     2 recip/calls      rec_cal         1.41  0.0383   7.53     4
#> 3     3 tie/friendship   tie             1.85  0.00206  6.74     1
#> 4     4 recip/friendship rec_fri         1.71  0.00558  7.24     2
#> 5     5 same/gradeType   same_gra        0.927 0.357    7.01     6
#> 6     6 same/floor       same_flo        1.65  0.00860  6.92     3
```

Read the **per-effect rows**. The omnibus combination across effects is
computed but deliberately not printed: it has had no calibration study, and it
is dominated by its most extreme input in both directions.


``` r
plot(goldfish::test_gof(mod01ChoiceDiag))
```

## Did a coefficient drift?

`test_gof()` asks whether a contribution is evenly spread; `test_time()` asks
the directed version — whether the coefficient itself moved over the sequence.


``` r
goldfish::test_time(mod01ChoiceDiag)
#> ── <goldfishTimeTest> ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Model "DyNAM" · sub-model "choice" · backend "cpp"
#> 439 intervals, 439 dependent events; 6 effects tested.
#> Score test of a "identity" time trend in each coefficient.
#> # A tibble: 6 × 7
#>   index term             coefficient statistic    df   p_value  rank
#>   <int> <chr>            <chr>           <dbl> <int>     <dbl> <int>
#> 1     1 inertia/calls    inrt           3.68       1 0.0551        5
#> 2     2 recip/calls      rec_cal        6.87       1 0.00878       4
#> 3     3 tie/friendship   tie           17.6        1 0.0000278     2
#> 4     4 recip/friendship rec_fri       18.7        1 0.0000153     1
#> 5     5 same/gradeType   same_gra       0.0554     1 0.814         6
#> 6     6 same/floor       same_flo       8.81       1 0.00300       3
#> 
#> Joint test: chi-squared 34.02 on 6 df, p 6.665e-06.
```


``` r
plot(goldfish::test_time(mod01ChoiceDiag))
```

One caveat worth carrying away, because it decides whether these tests can see
anything at all: the default network statistics are **binary**, and a binary
statistic has no functional form to get wrong. Against a misspecified
functional form these tests have essentially no power on it — measured at the
null rate. Use `weighted = TRUE` where tie strength is part of the hypothesis.
The diagnostics vignette shows the measurement.
